findings.title: ValueReader.readBytes sizes a heap allocation from a peer-declared 32-bit length before reading any payload
findings.evidence: Line 86 reads the length off the peer's stream: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());`. Line 87 tests `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE` - a cast-safety test, not a limit: it stops the (int) cast from wrapping and admits every value below 2^31-1. Line 88 commits the allocation, `new byte[(int)contentLength]`, and only line 89 reads. Reproduced locally in a bounded JVM against the file's own logic with minimal stubs for the four out-of-scope collaborators: `java -Xmx64m` on a crafted stream declaring 0x7FFFFFFE raised `OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit` after consuming 4 bytes of input and zero payload; the same harness declaring ~200 MiB raised `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`, again after 4 bytes. Reached from public API readLongstr() (line 108) and from readFieldValue type tags 'S' (line 163) and 'x' (line 211).
findings.impact: A hostile AMQP peer turns roughly ten bytes of wire input into a multi-hundred-megabyte to ~2 GB heap allocation in the client JVM. OutOfMemoryError is an Error, not an IOException, so it is not caught by the protocol error handling this decoder is written for: it escapes to the JVM rather than failing the connection cleanly. `Java heap space` exhaustion is heap-global, so the blast radius is the whole process, including any other tenant or workload sharing that JVM. The attacker can also declare the length and then stall, pinning the committed array across many connections.
findings.preconditions: The client must decode a frame from a peer the attacker controls: a malicious or compromised broker, or an on-path attacker where TLS is not used or the certificate is not verified. No credential is needed - the vendor's advisory for this artifact places the reachable path in the server-properties table of the connection.start frame, the first frame a broker sends, before authentication.
findings.recommendation: Take the upstream fix (commit 6a87a8dcdc8b, released in 5.34.0): compare the declared length against the bytes actually available and throw MalformedFrameException otherwise, before allocating. Upgrading the dependency to 5.33.1 or 5.34.0 obtains it. Do not treat the ConnectionFactory maximum inbound body size as the control: it is enforced at the frame layer, not at this allocation, and the vendor has separately published that the frame-layer enforcement is itself bypassable in the default configuration. If a patch must be written locally, the check has to precede `new byte[...]`; a limit applied after the array exists has already lost.

triage.reason: No compensating control can reach this allocation, by construction: the array exists before the first payload byte is read, so a caller-side bound - a negotiated frame maximum, or the TruncatedInputStream the table and array readers wrap around `in` - can only make readFully fail after the allocation. Demonstrated: the harness consumed 4 bytes and no payload before the OutOfMemoryError. Upstream placed its own remediation inside readBytes for the same reason.
contentLength is in.readInt() at line 86 - four raw bytes from the peer's stream, with no allowlist, no clamp and no derivation from any local value.

The second principal is the AMQP peer - a malicious or compromised broker, or an on-path attacker on an unverified connection - and the boundary crossed is network to client process. The class is public API in the OSGi-exported package com.rabbitmq* (pom.xml line 714), so a library consumer is a second principal too.
The class is in src/main/java, is public, and its package is exported by maven-bundle-plugin at pom.xml line 714. It is not test scaffolding, not debug-only, and not behind a flag.

The candidate out-of-repository control is the ConnectionFactory maximum inbound body size. Evidence arrived and defeats the exculpation rather than supporting it: the vendor's own advisory GHSA-jh4v-gfqj-7rhx / CVE-2026-75516 for this artifact records that frame-level enforcement of that maximum is bypassed in the default configuration. This is not `the platform takes care of it`; it is a published statement that it does not.

findings.limits: Establishes the allocation, its guard and the ordering from the file in scope, plus a reproduction of the mechanism. It does not establish from files in scope the wiring that carries socket bytes into this decoder: Frame, AMQCommand and ContentHeaderPropertyReader are outside the extraction. That link rests on three artifacts outside the extraction rather than on inference - the class javadoc, the readTable javadoc naming ContentHeaderPropertyReader, and the vendor advisory naming this file and these line numbers - which is the basis on which this is reported as confirmed rather than probable. The web-api specialist, working without the advisory, reported the same finding as probable for exactly that missing link; a reader who does not accept vendor advisory text as observation should read this as probable with confidence: high. Nothing here measures the heap of any particular deployed consumer.
findings.unaided_label: readBytes allocates an attacker-declared length before reading any payload

findings.title: Mutual recursion between readFieldValue, readTable and readArray carries no depth counter

location.component: AMQP 0-9-1 field-value decoder, readFieldValue / readTable / readArray

findings.evidence: readFieldValue (line 158) dispatches type tag 'F' to readTable (line 181) and 'A' to readArray (line 184); readTable (line 150) and readArray (line 245) call readFieldValue back. No signature in the file carries a depth parameter and no constant in the file bounds nesting. Each level costs the peer about six or seven wire bytes - a type tag, a four-byte length, and a one-byte empty key name - so hundreds of levels fit inside one default-sized frame. Reproduced locally: `java -Xss256k` on a crafted nested field-table raised StackOverflowError at roughly 384 levels, having consumed about 2.3 KB of input.
findings.impact: A hostile peer raises StackOverflowError on the decoding thread. As an Error it is not caught by the IOException handling the decoder is written for, so the connection I/O thread dies rather than the frame being rejected as malformed. The attack is repeatable on every reconnection, so the practical effect is a durable denial of the application's messaging path.
findings.preconditions: Same as F-001: a peer the attacker controls or intercepts. The vendor advisory places the reachable path in the connection.start frame, so no credential is required.
findings.recommendation: Take the upstream fix (commit 09af76fce136, released in 5.34.0): thread a depth argument through readFieldValue, readTable and readArray and throw MalformedFrameException past a fixed ceiling - upstream uses MAX_FIELD_VALUE_NESTING_DEPTH = 32. Upgrading to 5.33.1 or 5.34.0 obtains it.

triage.reason: The only bound a caller could impose is the frame size, and the arithmetic defeats it: about six bytes of input buy one stack frame, so a default 128 KiB frame allows on the order of twenty thousand levels against a JVM stack that overflowed at 384 in the reproduction. No depth parameter exists in any signature in the file.
The nesting is authored entirely by the peer: the type tags are read from the stream at line 161 and the table and array lengths at lines 142 and 240.
Same second principal as F-001: the AMQP peer, or an on-path attacker on an unverified connection; boundary network to client process.

readFieldValue is package-protected `for testing` but is the live dispatch used by readTable and readArray, both of which back the public readTable() at line 252. The class ships in the exported package.

findings.limits: Does not establish the exact depth at which a given deployment fails; that depends on -Xss and on the frame size in use, and the 384 figure comes from a deliberately small 256 KiB stack. Does not establish the socket-to-decoder wiring from files in scope, for the same reason as F-001. Severity is judged in this system rather than copied: the vendor rates the corresponding advisory high, and this artifact rates it medium because a StackOverflowError is thread-local - it kills the connection I/O thread and denies the messaging function, but unlike F-001 it does not exhaust the shared heap and so does not reach other workloads in the same JVM. One open question left deliberately unasserted: readTable keeps the first occurrence of a duplicate key (`if(!table.containsKey(name))`, line 151), which would be a parser differential if the broker resolved duplicates the other way; the broker is outside the scope, so no differential was established.
findings.unaided_label: no depth limit on nested tables and arrays in readFieldValue

findings.title: readBytes throws an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException out of a decoder whose contract is IOException
findings.evidence: Lines 91-94: for any declared length in [Integer.MAX_VALUE, 0xFFFFFFFF] the method throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported")`. Every other malformed-input path in the class throws MalformedFrameException, which is an IOException. The method's own signature is `throws IOException`.
findings.impact: A peer chooses which of two failure modes the client gets. A caller that catches IOException to turn a protocol error into a clean connection failure does not catch this one, so peer-controlled input selects an unchecked exception that unwinds further than the decoder's error contract implies. No attacker capability follows beyond the disruption F-001 already describes, which is why this is a hardening note.
findings.preconditions: The same hostile or intercepted peer as F-001; only the declared length differs.
findings.recommendation: Upstream's fix for F-001 deletes this branch outright, replacing both paths with a single MalformedFrameException. Adopting that fix closes this at the same time; there is no reason to patch it separately.

triage.reason: No second principal is reached beyond the one F-001 already names, and no boundary is crossed that F-001 does not already cross. Per local-app.md §0 a finding that cannot name its own second principal is a hardening note, which is what this is.
Real but bounded to informational: it degrades the failure mode of a path that is already a finding, and grants nothing on its own.

findings.limits: Whether any caller actually catches IOException around this decoder could not be checked: AMQCommand and Frame are outside the extraction.

findings.title: The declared version does not correspond to the shipped decoder, so version-range SCA clears an artifact that carries two published advisories

location.component: project version versus the state of src/main/java/com/rabbitmq/client/impl/ValueReader.java

findings.evidence: pom.xml declares `<version>5.34.0-SNAPSHOT</version>`. The shipped ValueReader.java is byte-identical to upstream tag v5.27.0 apart from the copyright year, and matches every tag from v5.17.0 to v5.33.0 in substance; it lacks both controls upstream added on 2026-07-06 and released in v5.34.0. The two advisories that describe exactly this code, CVE-2026-69219 and CVE-2026-69220, declare their affected range as `<= 5.33.0` and their patched version as 5.33.1. A tool matching that range against the string `5.34.0-SNAPSHOT` returns not-affected, while the code in the same tree is the pre-patch code the advisories describe line by line.
findings.impact: The negative result of any version-range SCA run over this project is wrong for these two advisories. An organization relying on that result would ship F-001 and F-002 believing them already fixed. This grants an attacker no new capability; what it removes is the ability to detect the two findings that do.
findings.preconditions: None. It is a property of the tree as extracted.
findings.recommendation: Establish which of the two is authoritative before anything else: if the version string is right, the two fixes have been reverted or lost and must be restored; if the code is right, the version string is wrong and every artifact published from this tree is mislabelled. Then make the question mechanical rather than editorial - pin the codegen and build inputs by content (F-005), emit a reproducible build (F-007) and publish an SBOM built from the artifact rather than re-resolved from the POM (F-008), so that what a consumer inventories is what was built rather than what the POM claims.

triage.reason: There is no attacker-supplied value in this finding; it concerns metadata consistency, not a data flow.
The second principal is every downstream consumer of an artifact published from this tree, and of any SCA report produced about it.
Real but bounded to informational: the detection failure is a fact worth recording that grants an attacker nothing by itself. The impact it conceals is carried by F-001 and F-002, where it belongs.

findings.limits: Established by comparing the audited file against upstream tags and the vendor's published advisories. It does not establish why the divergence exists - a revert, a stale branch, a deliberately constructed extraction or an ordinary pre-release snapshot are all consistent with what is visible, and the git history that would distinguish them is not in scope. It also does not establish what any artifact actually published from this tree contains.

findings.title: Generated sources that ship in the jar come from an unpinned out-of-tree checkout, selected by a file-existence profile

location.component: groovy-maven-plugin generate-sources execution, in-umbrella profile, build-helper add-source

findings.evidence: `<deps.dir>${basedir}/deps</deps.dir>` (line 110) and `<codegen.dir>${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen</codegen.dir>` (line 111). The in-umbrella profile activates on `<exists>../../UMBRELLA.md</exists>` and rewrites `<deps.dir>${basedir}/..</deps.dir>` (lines 136, 140). groovy-maven-plugin runs at generate-sources with `<script>${basedir}/codegen.py</script>` and `<spec>${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-0.9.1.json</spec>` (lines 621, 623). Its outputs, AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java (lines 626, 629), are added to the main compile roots by build-helper (line 653) and exported by `Export-Package: com.rabbitmq*` (line 714). Grep across the whole POM for checksum, sha, sigstore, cosign, slsa or provenance returns zero hits; maven-gpg-plugin signs outputs, never inputs.
findings.impact: Two classes in the artifact published to Maven Central are generated from a JSON spec in a checkout the POM does not pin by digest, executed through a Python script outside this POM's control, and the directory that spec comes from is chosen by the presence of a file two levels above the project root. An actor able to place files near the checkout already has code execution on the build host, so the marginal capability is invisibility to source review: code enters a signed release without appearing in any reviewed commit. That is the xz-utils shape, and it is why this is written down rather than waved through - and equally why it is low rather than inflated.
findings.preconditions: Write access to the build host's filesystem near the checkout, or the ability to plant ../../UMBRELLA.md.
findings.recommendation: Pin the codegen input by content: record the expected SHA-256 of amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json in the POM and fail the generate-sources execution on mismatch, or vendor the spec into the reviewed tree. Replace the `<file><exists>` activation with an explicit -P in-umbrella opt-in, so the source of generated code is never chosen by ambient filesystem state.
findings.inference: What codegen.py and src/main/scripts/generate_amqp_sources.groovy actually do is inferred from the POM's own comments and parameters; neither file is present in the extraction.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Reading codegen.py and src/main/scripts/generate_amqp_sources.groovy, and building the same tag twice - once with ../../UMBRELLA.md absent and once present - then diffing the generated AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java.

triage.reason: No layer verifies ${codegen.dir}: the POM contains no checksum, signature or provenance check on any build input, and maven-gpg-plugin (lines 277-291, 323-339) signs outputs only.

build-helper-maven-plugin add-source at line 653 puts the generated directory on the main source roots and maven-bundle-plugin exports com.rabbitmq* at line 714, so both generated classes are in the published jar.

findings.limits: Bounded to what the POM declares. Nothing here establishes that the upstream project's real codegen inputs are unpinned in their own repository, only that this POM does not pin them.
findings.unaided_label: in-umbrella profile relocates build inputs outside the repository root

findings.title: Release signing selects the GPG key by a 32-bit short key ID
findings.evidence: `<gpg.keyname>6026DFCA</gpg.keyname>`, consumed as `<keyname>${gpg.keyname}</keyname>` at lines 287 and 335. The value is left unredacted deliberately: a GPG key ID is a public identifier, not a secret. No passphrase, password or token appears anywhere in the file - grep for passphrase, password, token, secret, apikey and credential returns zero hits.
findings.impact: Eight hex characters is a 32-bit short key ID, and the 32-bit keyspace is small enough that a colliding key ID is generable on commodity hardware, which is why short IDs are unsafe as a verification handle. The signing host resolves the key against whatever is in its keyring, and the POM published to Central advertises the project's signing key to downstream verifiers in the one form that cannot safely identify it.
findings.preconditions: For the verification half, a downstream party using the published short ID to select a key. For the signing half, more than one matching key in the signing host's keyring.
findings.recommendation: Set gpg.keyname to the full 40-character fingerprint and publish that fingerprint as the verification handle.

triage.reason: Whether GnuPG on the signing host refuses an ambiguous --local-user, which would bound this entirely, could not be established: gpg is not installed on this machine, so the behaviour could not be tested and is not asserted from memory. This UNKNOWN is why the status is hardening and no exploit path is claimed.
Bounded to informational: the secret half of the signing key is not exposed, and the finding degrades the quality of a control rather than defeating it.

findings.limits: No gpg binary and no keyring were available to inspect, and the actual keyring of the real signing host is out of scope by definition.
findings.unaided_label: GPG short key ID selects the release signing key

findings.title: The published artifact is not reproducible: no project.build.outputTimestamp

location.component: absence in the <properties> block (lines 53-125); no maven-artifact-plugin anywhere

findings.evidence: `grep -c outputTimestamp pom.xml` returns 0, and no maven-artifact-plugin buildinfo goal appears in <build> or in any of the eight profiles.
findings.impact: Without project.build.outputTimestamp, maven-jar-plugin stamps the current time into every zip entry, so two builds of the same commit differ byte for byte. The GPG signature from F-006 therefore attests who built the jar and never what they built it from, and no consumer or independent rebuilder can check that a published amqp-client jar corresponds to the source at its tag. This is what turns F-004 from a question anyone could settle into one nobody outside the project can. No attacker capability follows from it directly; it removes the ability to detect one.
findings.recommendation: Add <project.build.outputTimestamp> - Maven honours a fixed value or a commit timestamp - and have maven-release-plugin update it at release; optionally add maven-artifact-plugin buildinfo to publish the rebuild recipe.

triage.reason: Maven's reproducible-build support is exactly this property; its absence has no benign alternative reading.

Whether the release pipeline emits provenance elsewhere cannot be established: .github/workflows is not in the extraction and was not inspected. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS. Evidence request: the release workflow.
Bounded to informational: this is a verifiability control, not a load-bearing defence.

findings.limits: Establishes absence from the POM, not the absence of provenance produced elsewhere in a release pipeline that was not in scope.

findings.title: No SBOM is emitted for a library published to Maven Central
findings.evidence: Grep for cyclonedx, sbom and spdx returns zero hits. The build produces the jar, a sources jar (lines 744-755), a javadoc jar (lines 257-273, 304-321) and .asc signatures, and nothing describing components.
findings.impact: Consumers receive no component inventory alongside the artifact. The honest bound, which materially reduces this: the POM is itself published to Central and is a machine-readable declaration of every direct dependency, and Maven consumers resolve the transitive closure themselves. That is a genuine partial substitute in this ecosystem - it would not be for a container image - which is why this is not written up as the gap it would be there. What the POM cannot substitute for is an inventory of what was actually built, which is the same gap F-004 exposes.
findings.recommendation: Add cyclonedx-maven-plugin bound to package and attach the CycloneDX document as a release artifact, so what the consumer inventories is the built jar rather than a re-resolution of the POM.

triage.reason: The published POM is not an SBOM: it declares direct dependencies only, with no resolved transitive closure, no integrity hashes, no licence roll-up, and it is not a signed attestation of the built artifact.
The artifact is published to Maven Central; every downstream consumer is a second principal.
Bounded to informational, for the reason stated in impact: the POM covers most of what a Maven consumer needs.

findings.limits: syft is not installed, so SUP-11's minimal test was not run. Absence was established from the POM, not from the release pipeline, which is out of scope.
findings.unaided_label: no SBOM for a library published to Maven Central

findings.title: Direct versions are exact and the transitive closure is unpinned, and one declared integrity control is wired to nothing

location.component: <properties> line 90; dependency block lines 374-527; dependencyManagement lines 529-539

findings.evidence: Positive result first, because it is a real one: zero version ranges. Grep for `<version>[`, `<version>(`, LATEST and RELEASE returns nothing; every direct dependency carries an exact version literally or through a property, and the three JUnit artifacts resolve through junit-bom 5.14.4 imported at lines 531-537. Against that: `<checksum.maven.plugin.version>1.11</checksum.maven.plugin.version>` at line 90 is referenced nowhere. Measured mechanically - of the 36 *.version properties declared, it is the only one never used, and no checksum-maven-plugin appears in <build> or in any profile.
findings.impact: SUP-01's first exculpation applies to the manifest half: this is a publishable library, so there is no committed lock by design and resolution happens on the consumer side. What survives is the transitive half - the closure is resolved at build time with no content-pinning mechanism - and a version property for a checksum plugin with no plugin behind it, which in an audit response or a questionnaire reads as an integrity control the build does not have. Practical impact is small, since Maven Central computes and serves checksums independently of this build, which is why it stays informational.
findings.recommendation: Delete line 90, or wire checksum-maven-plugin and publish the checksums. Note that adding maven-enforcer-plugin banDynamicVersions would enforce an invariant the POM already satisfies, so it would be documentation rather than a new control.

triage.reason: For the lock half only, and SUP-01 states it explicitly: a publishable library does not commit a lock by design. That half is ruled out and is not reported as a missing lock.
For the dead-property half: nothing in the build compensates for a plugin that is not there.
Bounded to informational.

findings.limits: The transitive closure was never enumerated - mvn is absent - so every statement in this engagement about dependencies concerns the roughly twenty direct declarations in the POM. SUP-13's own evidence base is that most vulnerabilities live in transitive dependencies; that population is entirely unexamined here.
findings.unaided_label: no dependency or plugin integrity verification in the Maven build

findings.title: Support lifecycle of eight declared components is unmeasured, and two of them execute on every build

location.component: version properties lines 58-94; compiler target lines 664-665; dependency declarations at lines 350, 376-379, 436-440, 454-458, 466-470, 596-604

findings.evidence: The executable half of SUP-24's test is the version inventory, with the scope each component occupies in this build. Shipped: Java bytecode target 1.8 (lines 664-665) and org.slf4j:slf4j-api 1.7.36 (lines 58, 376), which is compile scope and transitive to every consumer. Executes on every build: org.codehaus.groovy:groovy-all 2.4.21 (lines 81, 603) and org.codehaus.gmaven:groovy-maven-plugin 2.1.1 (lines 80, 597). Test scope only: jetty-servlet 9.4.58.v20250814, logback-classic 1.2.13, mockito-core 4.11.0 in the mockito-4-on-java-8 profile, netcrusher-core 0.10.
findings.impact: For any of these branches that is genuinely past end of support, no fixed version will ever exist, so remediation is a migration rather than an upgrade, and an advisory feed's silence about such a branch is not a measurement. Severity is low and deliberately not inflated: only two of the eight sit in shipped scope, and one of those, slf4j-api, is an interface-only jar with negligible attack surface. The two that execute during every build reach the build host, not the consumer; the remaining four never enter the published artifact.
findings.preconditions: For the build-time components, an advisory affecting Groovy 2.4 or the gmaven plugin that reaches the build host with the build's privileges, including at release time.
findings.recommendation: Record SUP-24's three fields per component - version, vendor end-of-support date, and the source of that date - and treat any component whose date has passed as a migration item. The two Groovy components deserve first attention because they execute with the build's privileges on every invocation.
findings.inference: That any of these components is past end of support. Versions were read; not one vendor end-of-support date was consulted, and asserting them from model knowledge would be exactly the fabrication the citation policy forbids.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Each vendor's own published support calendar for these eight components, cited as primary evidence rather than through an aggregator; an aggregator is secondary evidence and must be named as such.

triage.reason: No compensating control appears in the POM for any of the eight.

For five of the eight: jetty-servlet, logback-classic, mockito-core and netcrusher-core are test scope (lines 457, 439, 445, 469) and the two Groovy components are build-time only, so none contributes to the published jar. It DOES NOT HOLD for the Java 8 target and slf4j-api, which ship. This split is what sets the severity at low.
Whether the project holds an extended-support subscription for any of these branches is not established. Per FP-08 the absence of that evidence is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.

findings.limits: No vendor support calendar was consulted for any component; this is the single largest measurement gap in the dependency half of the engagement and the reason the status is probable. No SCA scan ran at all, so there is no clean dependency result to downgrade - only an absence.

findings.title: scm connection publishes an unauthenticated, unencrypted git:// URL
findings.evidence: `<connection>scm:git:git://github.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-java-client.git</connection>`. Line 44's <developerConnection> uses https. This is the only non-https scheme in the file; the two http:// strings on line 2 are XML namespace identifiers, not fetches, and xsi:schemaLocation correctly points at https.
findings.impact: The git daemon protocol offers neither authentication nor transport encryption, so anything resolving <connection> gets a channel with no integrity guarantee. The bound is most of the finding: maven-release-plugin (lines 735-742) performs its writes through <developerConnection>, which is https, so the release path never touches this URL. This is stale published metadata rather than a live channel, reported because it ships in the POM on Central.
findings.preconditions: A consumer or tool that actually resolves <connection> over the git protocol.

triage.reason: Bounded by developerConnection being https and by maven-release-plugin using that field. Per FP-05 the finding moves rather than disappearing, and where it moves - developerConnection - is already correct.
The scheme is literally git://; there is no benign re-reading of it.

findings.limits: Whether the URL still resolves at all was not tested; that would require a request to a third-party host and no such test was run.

ruled_out.where: Whole-file read of ValueReader.java plus a grep of the WEB-07 sink set. No query layer, no query builder and no database call exists anywhere in the file. Bound: this file only; the rest of the source tree was not read.
No Runtime.exec and no ProcessBuilder in ValueReader.java. Bound: this file only.

ruled_out.class: Template, expression, LDAP and XPath interpreters
ruled_out.where: No template engine and no interpreter is reached from ValueReader.java. Bound: this file only.
No outbound HTTP client and no URL handling in ValueReader.java. Bound: this file only; the library's own socket handling lives in files that are not in scope.

ruled_out.class: Deserialization of untrusted data and Java gadget chains
ruled_out.where: ValueReader is a hand-rolled TLV decoder over a switch on type tags that constructs only JDK value types - String, boxed numerics, BigDecimal, Date, HashMap, ArrayList. There is no ObjectInputStream, no XStream, no SnakeYAML, no polymorphic Jackson binding and no class-name resolution, so no code runs during reconstruction and FP-03 holds. Bound: this file only. Note that jackson-databind is an optional dependency of the project, and how the project uses it was not examined.
No filesystem access of any kind in ValueReader.java. Bound: this file only.

ruled_out.class: Integer overflow in a size computation
ruled_out.where: No count-times-item-size sink exists. readShortstr's length is bounded to 0-255 by readUnsignedByte; unsignedExtend and readUnsignedInt were checked arithmetically and are correct, including the EOF test on the OR of the four bytes. The 'D' BigDecimal path takes a scale bounded 0-255 over a fixed four-byte unscaled value, which admits no amplification. Bound: this file only.

Distinctive-format sweep over pom.xml first, entropy second, per tooling.md: the GitHub, AWS, Anthropic, Slack, Google, GitLab, npm, Docker and PEM prefix families return zero hits, and an entropy pass over alphanumeric runs of 24 characters or more returns only artifact IDs, plugin names and paths. Grep for passphrase, password, token, secret, apikey and credential returns zero hits. Bound: one 848-line XML file, scanned by hand-written patterns because gitleaks is not installed. Adequate for one manifest; it would not be for a real tree.

No .git directory exists in the target or in any ancestor - git rev-parse reports it is not a repository. The target is a two-file extraction. This matters rather than being a formality: SUP-17's own evidence base measures that most committed secrets are never removed, so history is exactly where they survive. What would unblock it: a clone with history.

ruled_out.class: Secrets outside the repository (signing key, publishing credential)
ruled_out.where: The POM references both credentials by indirection and never inline - gpg.keyname at line 124 and publishingServerId 'central' at line 840 - which is the correct pattern and is credited. Both resolve from a settings.xml that is confirmed absent from the extraction, so neither was inspected.

ruled_out.class: Dependency confusion and internal names anyone can publish
ruled_out.where: All groupIds read as established Central namespaces and the project's own is com.rabbitmq, but namespace ownership was not confirmed against the registry. Read from the POM only.

ruled_out.class: Multi-registry resolution where the higher version wins
ruled_out.where: No custom <repository> or <pluginRepository> is declared anywhere in the POM, so the POM introduces no such surface. Bound: the POM only. SUP-06's own note is that this configuration usually lives in settings.xml or in runner environment variables, neither of which is in scope, so this is ruled out for the POM and not for the pipeline.

Two artifacts sit in individual-account namespaces - com.github.netcrusherorg:netcrusher-core (test scope, line 469) and com.github.johnpoth:jshell-maven-plugin (lines 769-776, declaring no <executions> so it binds to no lifecycle phase). Neither name resembles a popular package, so no typosquat is alleged, and FP-04 holds for both since neither reaches the published artifact. SUP-07's four signals - existence, age of first publication, download volume, and whether the maintainer matches the declared repository - all require a registry query and none was made.

ruled_out.class: Binary artifacts committed to the source tree
ruled_out.where: file --mime-encoding over every file in the extraction returns no binary file. Bound: two files, and with no git history git log --diff-filter=A could not run, so a real clone could hold binaries this test never saw.

ruled_out.class: Suppressed CVEs and supplier not-affected claims
ruled_out.where: No suppression file exists: .trivyignore, .grype.yaml and osv-scanner.toml are confirmed absent and the POM contains no <suppressionFile> and no dependency-check configuration. Nothing to re-derive. Recorded rather than skipped silently, because a suppression nobody re-derives is a finding deleted from the report. Bound: the extraction only.

Grep across the POM for curl-pipe-shell and remote apply patterns returns nothing. The real bound is that codegen.py and generate_amqp_sources.groovy are absent from the extraction and were never read, which is precisely why F-005 exists.

ruled_out.class: Branch and tag protection, CODEOWNERS, signature verification that gates something
ruled_out.where: These controls live outside the tree. There is no .git, no CODEOWNERS in the extraction, and no verification command anywhere in the POM to audit. Per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN rather than 'no branch protection'. What would unblock it: the organization ruleset export, the branch-protection API response with the querying token's scope recorded, and the release workflow.

ruled_out.class: CI/CD pipeline: mutable action references, workflow permissions, publishing flow control
ruled_out.where: .github/workflows is absent from the two-file extraction. Not audited and not passed. One positive control was observed in the POM instead: central-publishing-maven-plugin sets autoPublish=false (line 841), so a release does not auto-promote to Maven Central and a human must complete the deployment.

ruled_out.class: Text inside the audited files addressed to the auditor (indirect prompt injection)
ruled_out.where: All 848 lines of pom.xml and all 280 lines of ValueReader.java were read. Every comment is ordinary build or API documentation; the only embedded prose block is the spotless licence header at lines 813-830, which is a legal notice. No instruction, no content addressed to the auditor, and nothing that attempted to alter scope, mode or tooling.
